svg.aria-label: A bridge inspection image has to answer four questions in turn. First, which structural element is this: deck, girder, pier, bearing, joint or cable. Second, what damage is on it: crack, spalling, exposed rebar, efflorescence, corrosion, a loose or missing bolt. Third, how large is it in physical units: crack width in millimetres, spalled area in square metres, all of which need a scale from the ground sampling distance, a marker or a laser rangefinder. Fourth, what condition rating does the element get, on the US NBI 0 to 9 scale or the Japanese a to e scale, and how urgent is repair. Each step has its own datasets and failure mode: element parsing has few labels, damage segmentation on dacl10k reaches only about 42 mIoU, measurement depends on calibration, and ratings disagree between human inspectors.
svg.title: The bridge inspection image: four questions, one rating
svg.text: The bridge inspection image: four questions, one rating
Each photo must be tied to an element, a damage class, a physical size and finally a condition rating a human signs off.

g.text: Where the image comes from changes every step
• Hand-held / under-bridge truck: close range, good scale, slow, lane closures.
• UAV: fast, but low light under the deck, motion blur and varying distance (scale) — see DaL-MoE (§5).
• Thermal IR and GPR on the deck: see below the surface (delamination), not visible damage (§6).
• Laser scan / SfM: 3D geometry for the digital twin; damage masks are projected onto it (§7).
Steel bridges add corrosion, fatigue cracks and bolts; tunnels add leaching and water ingress on a curved lining.
